extracted.intended_audience: poets, translators, literary critics, teachers of reading, and students of poetry/literature
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive and critical guidance on composing, translating, teaching, and judging poetry and poetic diction, drawn from Coleridge's Biographia Literaria (footnotes and commentary). Emphasizes taste, diction, metaphor, pedagogy, and language-specific constraints on translation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid premature or immoderate authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: “With the greatest possible solicitude avoid authorship. Too early or immoderately employed, it makes the head waste and the heart empty; even were there no other worse consequences. A person, who reads only to print, to all probability reads amiss; and he, who sends away through the pen and the press every thought, the moment it occurs to him, will in a short time have sent all away, and will become a mere journeyman of the printing-office, a compositor.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not publish or dispatch every passing thought. Allow ideas to be taken back into the mind, re-processed and re-secreted so that they retain vigour; constant immediate authorship produces exhaustion of thought and inferior workmanship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquire good taste by studying the best models
rubrics_metrics.description: “Good taste must be acquired, and like all other good things, is the result of thought and the submissive study of the best models. If it be asked, ‘But what shall I deem such?’--the answer is; presume those to be the best, the reputation of which has been matured into fame by the consent of ages.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate taste through deliberate study of canonical works whose merit has endured; rely on historically established models rather than passing fashions when learning standards of excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect language-specific poetic idiom when translating
rubrics_metrics.description: The Italian tongue has a language of poetry more distinct from prose than English; English 'demands a denser body of thought as the condition of a high polish' and the different genius of English discourages literal rendering of Italian poems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid literal or mechanical translations that ignore differences in poetic idiom and national 'genius'; adapt to the target language's requirements for diction, density of thought, and prosodic norms rather than slavishly reproducing source forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider prosodic and lexical differences across languages
rubrics_metrics.description: On average three English lines will express four German; German condenses meaning via compounds and prefixed participles, whereas English relies more on monosyllables/dissyllables and Latin derivatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When translating meter and lineation, account for difference in word-length, compounding, and syntactic habits; do not expect a one-to-one line correspondence—adapt meter and diction to the receiving language's capabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve precise meaning of terms (example: 'scene')
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'scene' should be kept to its original signification (theatre-related: scenery or the characters/actions presented on the stage) and not extended to a vague sense; avoid ambiguity produced by careless extension of meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer precise, historically grounded senses for evocative words; resist enlarging a word's meaning in ways that produce equivocation or weaken imagery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose words for precision and image (prefer stronger, specific phrasing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wordsworth’s judicious adoption of 'concourse wild' for 'a wild scene' is commended as an example of choosing words that supply precise imagery and honor poetic diction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select vocabulary that sharpens imagery and specificity rather than defaulting to vague or commonly worn phrases; small lexical shifts can markedly improve poetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid allowing poetry to approximate prose except where justified
rubrics_metrics.description: In many of Wordsworth's works the approximation of prose has been 'sedulously and on system guarded against'; the preface's theory justifies only rare instances where prose-like phrasing might be practicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a poetic diction distinct from ordinary conversation unless a narrator's voice or dramatic justification requires a prose-like turn; be deliberate when letting poetry resemble speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use diction consistent with speaker/narrator (character-appropriate language)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain words or phraseology (e.g., those 'not the phraseology of common conversation') are justified only by the narrator’s identity (the Vicar example); otherwise they feel incongruous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make elevated or unusual diction credible by tying it to a speaker's social standing, role, or narrative persona; avoid using language that undermines verisimilitude when no such justification exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure metaphors are contextually and physically appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: A metaphor that in one position is natural (Shakespeare’s wounded stag) may lose propriety in a different supposed position or context; misplaced metaphors become improper even if not strictly false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check that figurative language suits the physical circumstances and mental perspective represented; metaphors should arise naturally from context and not strain plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid needless or excessive repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: The author notes a writer’s peculiar habit of frequent repetition—many pages provide multiple instances—implying this is a stylistic fault rather than a virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guard against gratuitous repetition of phrases or images that dilutes force; use repetition deliberately for emphasis or structure, not by habit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate modes of oral expression in teaching reading
rubrics_metrics.description: It is an error to enforce reading 'as they would talk'—when children are made to repeat words from the book with eyes on the page their tones resemble talking, but this is an artificial effect; reciting written thoughts differs from uttering one’s own thoughts and requires a different mode of enunciation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach children appropriate modes for recitation versus conversational speech; avoid pedagogical techniques that produce mechanical, insincere delivery and thus harm natural feeling and expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pedagogical cruelties and humiliating remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism of Dr. Lancaster’s and Dr. Bell’s methods: methods that cure one extreme by introducing another (e.g., public shaming or mechanical caricature) are likely to have worse moral effects by hardening feeling and producing false ease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer teaching methods that respect pupils’ feelings and foster genuine expression; avoid punitive or humiliating practices in the name of correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of condensation vs unity in diction
rubrics_metrics.description: German (and Greek) ability to form compound words can condense rich meaning in single words; English gains some of that power via Latin derivatives but cannot replicate it entirely—concentration of sense (unity and simultaneousness) is valuable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for unity and simultaneity in expression (conciseness that preserves vividness) where appropriate, but recognize language limits and avoid awkward or unnatural compaction.
